n: Jehoshaphat returned home safely to Jerusalem — a mercy, since he had nearly died in Ahab’s place.
The prophet Jehu, son of the seer who had rebuked Asa, confronts Jehoshaphat: should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? God is displeased.
Yet God sees the good too: Jehoshaphat removed Asherah poles and set his heart to seek God. A rebuke and a commendation come together.

f.w: there are good things found in thee
prepared thine heart to seek God

n: Taking correction to heart, Jehoshaphat personally traveled from Beersheba in the south to Ephraim’s hills in the north, bringing people back to the Lord.

f.g: The full length of his kingdom, south to north.

n: He appointed judges in every fortified city of Judah — fitting for a king whose name means “the Lord judges.”
His charge to the judges: be careful, because you judge not for people but for the Lord, who is with you when you decide cases.

f.w: ye judge not for man, but for the LORD

n: Let reverence for God guide you, for God has no injustice, favoritism, or bribery. Judges must reflect God’s own character.
In Jerusalem he set up a higher court of Levites, priests, and family heads to decide religious matters and difficult disputes.
He charged them to serve with reverence, faithfulness, and a whole heart.
Whatever case comes from the towns — bloodshed, or questions of law and commandments — warn people so they don’t sin against the Lord and bring wrath on everyone.

f.g: Cases of homicide — deciding whether a killing was murder or accidental.

n: Amariah the chief priest would oversee religious matters and Zebadiah the king’s matters, with Levites as officers. Act courageously — the Lord will be with the good.

f.w: the LORD shall be with the good
